lede.headline: America votes tomorrow, and the Gulf is watching the calendar
lede.dek: Tuesday's midterms will decide who controls Congress. They may also mark the end of a pause in the confrontation with Iran.
body: Americans choose a new House and a third of the Senate on Tuesday 3 November. Democrats go in as favourites for the House and as slight favourites for the Senate, where Republicans hold 53 seats and Democrats need a net gain of four. Close to 50 million ballots were already cast before the weekend.

The vote matters well beyond Washington. Late last week Washington reportedly told Gulf governments to prepare for renewed strikes on Iran after the election, and oil rose on the news. Over the weekend Iran and Qatar floated a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US meets Tehran's conditions. Brent fell about 3% on Monday morning on that hope.
So the week has two clocks. One is the US election count. The other is whether the Doha channel turns into a deal before Washington's attention returns to the Gulf.
lede.oneBreath: America votes tomorrow, and the real question for us in the Gulf is whether the Hormuz talks in Doha produce something before Washington turns back to Iran.

glance: US midterms are tomorrow. Democrats are favoured for the House; the Senate is close to a coin toss, leaning Democratic in most forecasts.
Iran and Qatar have proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US lifts sanctions and meets other conditions. Trump says talks are going fine but he is in no hurry.
Israel's election ended in deadlock: Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48. Likud claims, without evidence, that the vote was stolen.
Hackers took about $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto theft on record. Blockchain analysts link it to North Korea.
Tech stocks are on a third losing week as investors question AI spending, with Apple, AMD and Palantir reporting this week.

stories.headline: Iran offers to reopen Hormuz in 48 hours, on its terms
stories.summary: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran and Qatari mediators have drafted a two-day plan. The US would act on day one, and Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restore normal shipping on day two. An earlier Iranian version took seven days.
stories.background: The US and Israel struck Iran on 28 February. A Pakistan- and Qatar-brokered memorandum in June paused the fighting, but it broke down in July and sanctions returned. Shipping through the strait has been heavily disrupted since the spring.
stories.whyItMatters: About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through Hormuz. Iran's conditions include lifting the post-July sanctions, reducing the US military presence in the region, restoring oil waivers and releasing frozen funds, some held in Qatar. Washington has not accepted them, and the US military maintains the strait is open.
stories.talkingPoint: The Doha plan is quicker than anything Tehran has offered before, but it is still a list of demands. The real signal is whether Washington moves on sanctions before or after the midterms.
stories.askThem: Do you think Washington would trade sanctions relief for shipping before the election is even counted?

stories.headline: Midterms tomorrow: the House leans Democratic, the Senate is the real contest
stories.summary: Forecasters give Democrats a strong chance of winning the House; Decision Desk HQ puts it at about 80%. The Senate is closer. Republicans hold 53 seats, Democrats need a net gain of four, and forecasts give them roughly a 57–78% chance depending on the model.
stories.background: Midterms usually punish the president's party. National polls have shown voters wanting a check on Trump. Mid-decade redistricting in several states should still hand Republicans a few new safe House seats.
stories.whyItMatters: A Democratic House would bring subpoenas, investigations and budget fights in 2027. A Democratic Senate would also limit Trump's appointments. Results in close Senate races such as North Carolina, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas may take days to finalise.
stories.talkingPoint: Watch the Senate, not the House. The House looks settled; the Senate turns on half a dozen races that are within the margin of error.
stories.askThem: If Democrats take the House, do you expect them to govern or mostly investigate?

stories.headline: Israel's election ends in deadlock, and Likud cries foul
stories.summary: Netanyahu's bloc won 53 of 120 seats and Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 48, leaving both short of the 61 needed. Three Arab-led parties won 19 seats. Likud says the vote was 'stolen'. Police say there is no supporting evidence, and the election committee says the results stand.
stories.background: An Eisenkot government with the Arab parties would have 67 seats, but Eisenkot has ruled that out. Avigdor Liberman will only back an all-Zionist coalition, possibly including Likud without Netanyahu.
stories.whyItMatters: Results must be certified by 4 November. President Herzog will then consult the parties and choose who gets the first attempt to form a government. Several analysts now think another election is the most likely outcome, with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker in the meantime.
stories.talkingPoint: Neither side can reach 61 without crossing a line it has sworn not to cross. That is why people are already talking about another election.
stories.askThem: Do you think Eisenkot would ever govern with Arab parties' support, even from outside the coalition?

stories.headline: Talk of a deal grows while the strikes get heavier
stories.summary: A Russian drone strike on Dnipro's main railway station killed at least 14 people. A short local truce allowed evacuees to leave occupied Oleshky, and it is now ending. Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian refineries.
stories.background: Trump has suggested a settlement could come before December's G20 summit in Miami. Rubio has doubted a quick deal. Zelensky says he will meet Putin in Türkiye and rejects Trump's claim that he is the one holding out.
stories.whyItMatters: Zelensky says Russia launched about 1,940 attack drones, 1,580 guided bombs and 44 missiles at Ukraine in the past week. The diplomacy and the fighting are moving in opposite directions, and Europe pays for both.
stories.talkingPoint: There is plenty of deal talk, but the strike numbers say both sides are still trying to improve their positions before any table is set.
stories.askThem: Would a Putin–Zelensky meeting in Türkiye mean anything without Trump in the room?

stories.headline: $6.3 billion gone from Binance in about twenty minutes
stories.summary: Hackers drained about $6.36 billion from Binance wallets across ten blockchains, mostly in roughly twenty minutes, according to TRM Labs, which calls it the largest crypto theft on record. TRM and Chainalysis link it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit.
stories.background: The FBI is investigating but has not publicly named North Korea; private analysts made that attribution. The FBI blamed the same group for last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit. Binance has frozen about $3 billion and says it will cover all losses.
stories.whyItMatters: This is now a sanctions and national-security story as well as a crypto one. Pyongyang uses stolen crypto to fund its weapons programmes. Binance's early finding of a compromised laptop, followed by 'additional points of breach', will worry every exchange.
stories.talkingPoint: This was a state operation against the world's biggest exchange, not a crypto heist in the usual sense.
stories.askThem: Does this change how you think about keeping money on exchanges?

stories.headline: Expensive oil, a hawkish Fed and doubts about AI weigh on markets
stories.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq have fallen for three weeks in a row as weak tech results revive doubts about AI spending. Brent was around $108–110 on Monday, down from $117 last week. The Fed held rates at 3.75–4.00%, and two officials voted for a hike.
stories.background: Goldman Sachs estimates that about $27 of the oil price is a war-risk premium. Under Chair Kevin Warsh the Fed has kept a patient tone, but markets are pricing a good chance of a December hike.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a busy week: the election on Tuesday, AMD results the same evening, Apple's first quarter under CEO John Ternus, then the US jobs report on Friday. Nvidia reports later in November.
stories.talkingPoint: The market has stopped paying for AI promises alone. It wants to see the returns, and $110 oil leaves it little patience.
stories.askThem: Do you think this is a pause in the AI trade or the start of a proper reset?

stories.headline: Canada wants to be the EU's first 'associate member'
stories.summary: Mark Carney told EU leaders in Montreal that Canada wants to become the bloc's first associate member, with talks finished by June. The word 'associate' does not appear in the summit's final statement, which commits both sides to define the relationship by 2027.
stories.background: Carney has been moving closer to Europe as US trade policy turns against Ottawa. Trump has called the plan a possible 'hostile act' and threatened tariffs on Europe.
stories.whyItMatters: This would create a new tier of EU membership, between partner and member. Germany is hesitant about the wording, so the label may change, but Canada's direction is clear.
stories.talkingPoint: Carney is trying to make Canada a European country in all but geography. Whether Berlin accepts the word 'associate' is the real test.
stories.askThem: If Canada can do it, who would be next — Norway, the UK?
stories.watch: Whether the EU formally adopts the 'associate' language, and Washington's response.

stories.headline: After 35 years, the UN's Western Sahara mission is in limbo
stories.summary: On 30 October the Security Council failed to renew MINURSO before its mandate lapsed. A US draft got only 3 votes in favour, 1 against and 11 abstentions, and a Russian alternative also failed.
stories.background: MINURSO was set up in 1991 to organise a referendum on independence that never took place. Last year's renewal endorsed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for a settlement. The US draft would have renamed the mission and dropped the word 'referendum'.
stories.whyItMatters: Losing the UN presence removes one of the few buffers in a dispute involving Morocco, Algeria and the Polisario Front. It also shows how hard it has become to get anything through the Council.
stories.talkingPoint: The UN mission created to hold a referendum has ended without one ever being held, which says a lot about where the issue now stands.
stories.askThem: Does Morocco now simply have the autonomy outcome it wanted?

stories.headline: Shenzhen prepares for a third Trump–Xi meeting this year
stories.summary: APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen on 18–19 November, and Trump and Xi are expected to hold their third meeting of the year. Trump will stop in the Philippines for the ASEAN summit on the way.
stories.background: Xi visited Washington in September, and the two leaders are also due to meet at the G20 in Miami in December. Trump has floated a three-way summit with Xi and Putin on 'denuclearization'. Beijing has not agreed to it.
stories.whyItMatters: Tariffs, chips, AI rules and Taiwan will all be on the table. About 1,000 business leaders attend the APEC CEO Summit alongside, with AI on the agenda and a 'Shenzhen Initiative' expected.
stories.talkingPoint: Three Trump–Xi meetings in a year is not a thaw, but it is steady contact, and markets have learned to trade on it.
stories.askThem: Is the US–China relationship being managed now, or just postponed?
stories.watch: Official confirmation of Trump's attendance and any announcement on the Xi–Putin summit idea.

careful.advice: Many people in the Gulf have family, business or travel affected by it. Ask how it touches them before giving your own view.
Say what the institutions have said: police found no supporting evidence and the election committee says the results stand. That keeps you factual without taking sides.
Ask people what they expect rather than what they want. You will learn more and start fewer arguments.
